The Cake That Quit

Luke rents a cottage, switches off his phone and bakes himself a birthday cake. A quiet day seems possible until the cake makes a run for it.

Read the whole storyMake one like this

Luke’s story

Read the story below, or open the page-turning reader.

A quiet birthday. That was the idea.

Luke had rented the cottage because he wanted one birthday without notifications, small talk or anybody asking what he was doing next. He turned off his phone, opened a bottle of something decent and baked a strawberry cake. Pip the fox watched from the doorway with the solemn focus of an auditor. Luke placed the final berry on top. “There,” he said. “One thing today has gone exactly to plan.” The cake gave a small, unmistakable hiccup.

Then it grew legs.

Two pink boots appeared beneath the sponge. The cake hopped off its stand, landed neatly, and ran through the open door. Luke remained still for a moment, partly from shock and partly because he had spent four hours on the icing. Pip was already halfway down the path. “Of course,” Luke said, grabbing his jacket. “The cake has boundaries.” Then he followed, leaving his silent phone on the kitchen table.

Lightly dusted.

The cake charged into the village bakery and slipped beneath a cooling rack. Luke did not. A ribbon of dough caught him across the chest while two bakers emptied bowls of flour in opposite directions. When the air cleared, Luke was white from eyebrows to trainers. Pip emerged looking equally powdered and far less embarrassed. Mrs Bell pointed a wooden spoon at the rear door. “Your dessert,” she said, “has ignored the one-way system.”

Things become less plausible.

In the bookshop, the cake squeezed behind a stack of atlases and left a pink handprint across Norway. Luke reached for it. The atlas snapped shut on his sleeve. Three hardbacks flapped off a shelf, circled his head and joined the cake on its way out. Mr Vale looked over his glasses. “I usually charge for damaged stock.” Luke freed himself. “Put it on the cake’s account.” Pip sneezed somewhere behind Travel.

The market gets involved.

The cake sprinted between market stalls, caught three falling oranges on its top tier and paused to bow. A crowd formed immediately. Someone began filming. Luke considered turning back, changing his name and moving abroad. Instead, he stepped over a basket of leeks and kept going. “Please don’t encourage it,” he called as the applause grew. The cake spun once, lost an orange, caught it again and ran on.

Nobody make this worse.

At the old stone bridge, the cake climbed onto the narrow wall. Six ducks gathered below with the professional patience of creatures expecting lunch. Luke slowed. The icing trembled in the breeze. Pip sat down and covered his eyes with both paws. “Nobody move,” Luke said. A tourist took a photograph. The cake tilted towards the water, recovered, then sprang to the opposite bank. The ducks complained loudly. Luke exhaled and began to suspect the escape had a destination.

The chase acquires catering.

The cake cut through a woodland picnic. Rabbits abandoned their sandwiches. Two mice seized the napkins. A hedgehog joined the pursuit without asking for context, which Luke respected. By now the bakers, bookseller, market crowd and six indignant ducks were close behind. Luke had wanted to avoid people for the day. Instead, he appeared to be leading a parade with refreshments. Pip glanced back at the growing crowd and looked extremely pleased with himself.

It was never escaping.

At sunset, the cake reached the empty village square and stopped beneath the lanterns. Luke arrived first, then everyone else tumbled in behind him. The cake turned slowly, as if checking attendance. That was when Luke understood. It had not run away from his birthday. It had collected one for him. “You could have left a note,” he said. The cake gave a proud wobble. Pip sat beside it, wearing the expression of somebody who had known all along.

Against all instinct, Luke accepts help.

The chase had cost the cake most of its icing, three strawberries and one pink boot. Mrs Bell produced cream. The market traders opened their berry baskets. The mice returned the missing boot, slightly chewed. Luke started to object, then stopped. He handed out spoons instead. Pip appointed himself Head Taster and found a paper hat to support the claim. For once, Luke let other people finish what he had started. The cake stood patiently in the middle of it all.

Quiet was overrated.

Under the lanterns, Luke cut the first slice. There was cake for the bakers, bookseller, traders, tourists, rabbits, mice, hedgehog and six ducks who insisted they had saved the day. His phone remained unanswered on the cottage table. Nobody asked what came next. Pip licked cream from his nose. The cake gave one last, tiny hiccup and the square burst into laughter. Luke had planned a quiet birthday. He decided not to be precious about it.
